text:
Helping researchers work with incomplete omics data through reproducible methods, realistic benchmarks and accessible software.

title: Missing value imputation
section: What does a missing measurement mean?
text:
What does a missing measurement mean?
An empty value in an omics dataset can have several explanations. A signal may fall below a measurement threshold, an instrument may not detect a feature consistently, or a value may be absent for another reason. Those differences matter when deciding how to analyse the data.
Imputation replaces missing entries with estimates. Different methods make different assumptions about the data and its missingness, so replacing every gap with the same simple value can change relationships among measurements. A useful evaluation considers both reconstruction and the consequences for subsequent analysis.

title: Missing value imputation
text:
Questions we explore

How do different patterns of missingness influence imputation performance?
How can researchers compare algorithms within a reproducible workflow?
What happens to downstream analysis after missing values are replaced?

title: Missing value imputation
text:
Our approach
We develop software that lets researchers compare imputation methods within a common workflow. The imputomics web application and R package bring multiple algorithms together and support benchmarking under different missingness scenarios.
Our focus is on making the comparison reproducible and accessible. Instead of treating one method as universally best, we examine performance in the context of a dataset, the simulated missingness and the question being asked. The linked publication story introduces the software and its evaluation framework.

title: Protein dynamics with HDX-MS
text: Turning hydrogen–deuterium exchange measurements into interpretable views of protein behaviour.

title: Protein dynamics with HDX-MS
text:
Proteins in motion
Protein function depends on more than a single structure. Hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS, measures changes in deuterium uptake over time and helps researchers investigate protein dynamics and differences between experimental states.
The resulting data have several dimensions: sequence position, exchange time, biological state, peptide charge and replicates. Analysing them together requires careful aggregation, quality control and an explicit treatment of uncertainty.

title: Protein dynamics with HDX-MS
text:
Questions we explore

How can complex measurements be summarised without losing their experimental context?
Which differences between protein states are supported by the data and their uncertainty?
What additional information can overlapping peptides provide about local protein dynamics?

title: Protein dynamics with HDX-MS
text:
Our approach
We develop tools that connect statistical analysis with visual exploration. HaDeX2 supports multidimensional analysis and visualisation of HDX-MS data, helping researchers examine coverage, measurement variability and differences between experimental conditions.
Our high-resolution work addresses the relationship between peptide measurements and more local estimates of deuterium uptake. HRaDeX explores residue-level uptake rates through kinetic modelling. These approaches provide complementary ways to interrogate the data, with the underlying assumptions remaining important to interpretation.

title: Antimicrobial peptides
text: From peptide sequences to reliable predictions: understanding what our models can tell us, and what still needs an experiment.

title: Antimicrobial peptides
text:
Small molecules, complex questions
Antimicrobial peptides are a diverse group of molecules studied for their ability to act against microorganisms. Their activity depends on sequence and molecular properties, but also on the organism and the conditions in which a peptide is tested. A single activity label can hide much of that context.
Computational tools can help prioritise sequences for further investigation. To be useful, however, their predictions need to hold up beyond the dataset used to build the model. That makes the choice of training examples, negative data and evaluation strategy central to the biological question.

title: Antimicrobial peptides
text:
Questions we explore

What distinguishes a useful peptide predictor from a model that performs well only on a familiar dataset?
How does the choice of negative examples influence a benchmark?
Where do predictions agree with experimental observations, and where do they fail?

title: Antimicrobial peptides
text:
Our approach
We develop and examine computational methods for peptide research, with a particular focus on fair evaluation and reproducibility. Our benchmarking work asks how the construction of negative datasets influences apparent model performance.
We also connect predictions with experimental testing. Our study of selected short amyloids predicted to be antimicrobial illustrates why a model score alone does not establish biological activity. Together, these projects help explain both the possibilities and the limits of sequence-based prediction.

title: Michał Burdukiewicz
text:
Biography
Hi! My name is Michał Burdukiewicz and I am passionate about bioinformatics and R.
I am currently leading the Laboratory of Bioinformatics and Multi-omics Analysis at the Medical University of Białystok. Contact me if you want to collaborate with us!
My current projects:

AmyloGraph, a comprehensive database of amyloid-amyloid interactions (doi:10.1093/nar/gkac882).
HaDeX, an integrated analytical tool for HDX-MS (maintainer Weronika Puchała).
Negative data sampling, where we show that benchmarks in antimicrobial peptide prediction are biased due to the selection of negative data (doi:10.1093/bib/bbac343).

I am also maintaining the list of machine learning models for prediction of peptide properties (see also our article on that).
I ❤️ R!

title: Find your way into BioGenies
text: Whether you have a question, an idea for a collaboration or a dataset to analyse, here is a path into our work.

title: Find your way into BioGenies
text:
For students

EXPLORE · LEARN · GET IN TOUCH

Find a question that interests you.
We work where biology, data analysis and programming meet. You can start with the science without already knowing every method.

Explore the questions. Read our research stories in plain language, then explore research topics.
Meet the people and their work. Browse the team and completed theses and dissertations for examples of research directions.
Start a conversation. Tell us about your interests, experience and the kind of project you would like to explore. Email BioGenies to ask about possibilities.

Try a five-minute missing-data demo →

title: Find your way into BioGenies
text:
For researchers & collaborators

SHARED QUESTIONS · COMPLEMENTARY EXPERTISE

Begin with the question you want to answer.
Our research connects protein aggregation, multiomics, statistical methods and machine learning. Existing projects and publications are a useful starting point for finding common ground.

Find a shared interest. Explore our research topics and project portfolio.
Find the relevant expertise. Meet the team and collaborators, and follow their publication links.
Bring an idea. Email the group with a short description of your question, available data or experiments, and the expertise you would like to connect.

Browse our publications →

title: Find your way into BioGenies
text:
For software & database users

EXPLORE · UNDERSTAND · APPLY

Find a resource for your next analysis.
Our catalogue includes web applications, R packages and curated biological databases. Each resource has its own scope and documentation.

Find a resource. Browse software and databases for links to applications and source code.
Understand the research behind it. Read the imputomics, AmyloGraph and HaDeX2 stories.
Try an idea before a full analysis. Use the missing-data sandbox to explore why estimates depend on the method and the missing values.

Open the software catalogue →

title: OneTick
text:
The research question
OneTick brings ecology, predictive modelling and biomedical research together within a One Health framework. The project connects the study of ticks, hosts and pathogens with biomarker discovery and public outreach, supported by international and interdisciplinary staff exchanges.

title: OneTick
section: What the project sets out to do
text:
What the project sets out to do


01 / RESEARCH AIM

Understand urban tick ecology
Assess tick abundance, diversity and pathogens, and model the relationships between ticks, hosts and disease spread (WP1–2).



02 / RESEARCH AIM

Connect biology and diagnostics
Investigate biomarkers and develop diagnostic models (WP3).



03 / RESEARCH AIM

Share knowledge and practice
Create public guidelines and educational campaigns (WP4). Support exchange through 90 person-months of secondments: 60 intersectoral and 30 interdisciplinary.

title: AMI-CryoML
text:
The research question
Amyloid fibrils can adopt different structures, and those differences matter for their biological effects. AMI-CryoML investigates how small aggregation modulators affect both aggregation kinetics and the structures that form. Linking experiments with structural data provides the basis for learning relationships that can be tested in predictive models.

title: AMI-CryoML
section: What the project sets out to do
text:
What the project sets out to do


01 / RESEARCH AIM

Map the modulators
Collect aggregation modulators and characterise their chemical and mechanistic properties.



02 / RESEARCH AIM

Measure and resolve
Use thioflavin-T assays to measure kinetic effects across prions, CsgA and α-synuclein, and cryo-EM to resolve fibril polymorphs.



03 / RESEARCH AIM

Connect data with prediction
Extend AmyloGraph with modulator–kinetics–structure records and train models to predict modulator effects.

title: Next stop, Geneva! Krysia is heading for a postdoc 🇨🇭🎓🚀
text:
🎉 Big news for Krysia! 🥹💚
Krysia will soon start a postdoctoral position at the University of Geneva, where she will work with Prof. Jeffrey Näf, an assistant professor at the University of Geneva who completed his PhD in statistics at ETH Zurich 🎓🤝
His research focuses on missing values, distributional prediction and robust estimation, topics concerned with learning from incomplete data, understanding more than a single predicted outcome and developing methods that remain reliable when assumptions do not quite match reality.
With Krysia’s work on evaluating missing value imputation methods, including Iscores, there is plenty of scientific common ground 💻⚖️.
New countries, new office but missing values are not getting rid of her that easily 😄

text:
Our lab had an amazing team retreat in Wrocław, packed with 🍕 pizza, 🎂 cake pops, forest adventures, board games and seminars, a mix of fun and productivity!




We kicked off our retreat with doing big groceries 🧺🍓🍉🥑🥦🍆

We ventured to the lush Arboretum Wojsławice (a stunning botanical garden near Niemcza) 🌳🌸🦋🪑

Highlights included:

A guided walk with the Arboretum director and UWr rector.



Hunting down collectible stamps around the trails—and earning prizes 🏅

Weronika, Krysia and Valen hugged a tree to absorb its positive energy 🌳💚

We also celebrated Valen’s and Eva’s birthdays 🎉 with cake and warm wishes—lots of smiles and shared joy! 🎂

Then we set off on a hike to Ślęża, through forests and past an old castle.  
Despite the castle’s dwindling water supply, the views were breathtaking, although Jarek died on the trail 🤭🫣







On the last day we had a brakefast together, with full bellies we went our ways.



Michał traveled to Łódź for doctoral school evaluations and later to Vilnius University

title: 🌟 Highlights from the 3rd ML4NGP Conference in Vilnius!🌟
text:
We have returned from the 3rd ML4NGP Meeting, top-tier conference on machine learning for non-globular proteins, held May 20–23 in vibrant city of Vilnius 🇱🇹.

From our team Michał, Jarek, Valen and Mariia actively proudly presented their posters and actively participated in engaging scientific discussions with global peers 🌍✨



What better way to start a scientific adventure than with a classic fuel-up at the iconic Golden Arches in Augustów, our always stop when visiting Vilnius? Our first stop was a hearty break for some quick, comfort food, because brilliant minds run on good food! 😋🍔




The very first evening brought a heartwarming reunion with colleagues from the Autonomous University of Barcelona 🇪🇸 and the Technical University of Denmark 🇩🇰 during a cozy dinner at London Grill restaurant. Great food, great company and lots of laughs! 🥂🍽️
 



The first day was packed with fascinating lectures, groundbreaking research and vibrant discussions. Every session challenged and inspired us to think deeper and push further, exactly what ML4NGP is all about 💡💻



The day ended at the historic Vilnius University main building with the Welcome Reception, followed by a fun evening at local food trucks. Party was top-notch! 🌇🎉🌮



One of the best parts of any conference is meeting incredible people and ML4NGP 2025 was no exception. We connected with inspiring researchers from Spain 🇪🇸, Germany 🇩🇪, Canada 🇨🇦, Armenia 🇦🇲, Italy 🇮🇹, Argentina 🇦🇷 and beyond! 🌐✨
Here’s a joyful group photo after our final lunch, a perfect snapshot capturing the spirit of collaboration and friendship forged over these unforgettable days 📸❤️




We’re incredibly grateful to have been part of such a dynamic and forward-thinking community. ML4NGP 2025 has fueled our passion and sparked new ideas that will shape our amyloid and LLPS work ahead.
Can’t wait to see what the next year holds! 🚀🔬💙

title: 🎉 Jarek awarded Horizon Europe ERA Talents grant!
text:
We’re thrilled to announce that Jarek has received a Horizon Europe ERA Talents Postdoctoral Fellowship! 🌟 This came as a surprise twist after he submitted a MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship proposal, which, while not funded, still passed all threshold points. For a first European-level application, that’s already a huge win! 💪
But here’s the plot twist: 💡 his application was automatically moved to the ERA Talents scheme. We had already lost hope…
…Until last week, out of the blue, we received a notification from the European Commission:

“Congratulations. Your proposal has reached the stage of Grant Agreement preparation.”


Cue the celebration! 🎊🥳🎊🥳🎊🥳


Starting early next year, Jarek will begin a two-year research stay at Vilnius University 🇱🇹. There, he’ll:

🔬 Study the impact of small molecules on amyloid polymorphism

🧩 Apply the findings to expand the AmyloGraph database

🤝 Collaborate closely with top researchers in the field

This project promises to push forward our understanding of amyloid structures and interactions and feed valuable insights into our growing infrastructure!


We’re incredibly proud of Jarek for this achievement and perseverance. From nearly missing out to scoring an amazing opportunity, this grant will open new doors for international collaboration and career development!

title: Welcome Mariia, from BTU to the BioGenies!
text:
We’re thrilled to introduce Mariia Solovianova to our lab! A biotechnology master’s graduate from BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg with solid wet lab experience 🧬, Mariia is here to dive into bioinformatics. Her first project? Collaborating with Valen and Ronja on amyloid aggregation modulators!



Mariia’s hands-on background in biotechnology will be gathering and organizing data on antibody-amyloid interactions. This project holds exciting potential for insights into therapeutic small molecule design and understanding amyloid diseases at a molecular level. As she transitions to bioinformatics, Mariia will bring her analytical skills into action with our team’s support.
Welcome aboard, Mariia! 🎉 We’re thrilled to have you in the BioGenies and excited to see the discoveries you and Valen will make together.

title: 🎉 Exciting news: Michał awarded NCN Sonata 19 Grant! 🎉
text:
We are proud to announce that Michał has been awarded the prestigious NCN Sonata 19 grant for his project titled “Taming aggregation with AmyloGraph 2.0: a database and prediction models of amyloid self-assembly modulators” 🧬✨
This innovative research will focus on expanding AmyloGraph, a comprehensive amyloid interactions database aimed at understanding and controlling the self-assembly of amyloid proteins. Michał’s work promises to make significant contributions to the field of protein aggregation, with potential implications for tackling diseases linked to amyloid formation.
We have planned three new positions for the project. Stay tuned for the announcement at the end of summer vacation!

text:
We are thrilled to announce the official beginning of our Bioinformatics and Multiomics Analysis Laboratory! 🚀
This state-of-the-art facility is dedicated to unlocking the mysteries of biological data through cutting-edge computational tools and integrative multiomics approaches.
Our mission is to empower researchers and scientists with the resources and expertise to analyze complex biological datasets, bridging the gap between raw data and meaningful insights. Whether it’s genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics, our lab is equipped to provide comprehensive analysis and innovative solutions.
Stay tuned for exciting research projects, collaborations, and workshops that will shape the future!

title: Come research with us
text:
In their own words


Eva about her Erasmus+ Mobility internship Oct 2024 - Jan 2025

My Erasmus experience in Białystok has been truly unforgettable, thanks to the amazing team I had the privilege to work with. From the very beginning, they made my integration seamless, even going the extra mile to set up a fully equipped kitchen, providing everything from casseroles to cutlery. Beyond that, they fostered a strong sense of fellowship by organizing regular team-building activities, such as trips and fun dinners together.
What really stood out, though, was how outstanding this team is in the field of Bioinformatics. They are not only highly active in conducting cutting-edge research with multiple ongoing projects and publications, but they also offer exceptional mentorship. Whenever I had doubts, they were always there to guide me, providing valuable insights that helped me improve my skills and grow as a researcher. This experience has truly been enriching, both personally and professionally.
BioGenies truly became my small Polish family during my time in Białystok.



Ronja about her Leonardo/Erasmus+ praxissemester Sep 2024 - Feb 2025

From the very first moment, I felt incredibly welcomed by the group—it was honestly amazing! Everyone was so kind and supportive, always ready to help with any research, answer my questions, or just be there whenever I needed something.
They organized so many fun activities to explore Białystok and the surrounding areas, making it really easy to get to know the city and meet new people. They also helped me with all the necessary paperwork, which was such a relief. Finding a place to stay was completely stress-free because they quickly helped me organize a flat in the student dorms. On top of that, they even provided kitchen necessities, so I didn’t have to buy anything for five months—such a thoughtful gesture!
One thing I truly appreciated was how much effort they put into helping me find a riding stable that suited me. Even though it turned out to be a bit difficult for me in the surrounding area, they still did everything they could to help, which meant a lot.
The work atmosphere here is just incredible. I always felt comfortable and knew I could trust everyone with any problem. It’s not just a group—it feels like a community where everyone looks out for each other. I couldn’t have asked for a better experience! Thank you for letting me stay with you!



Maria about her Erasmus+ Mobility internship Nov 2024 - Jun 2025

My Erasmus stay in Białystok has been an incredible experience so far! The group welcomed me with open arms, and they are always eager to teach me new things and help me grow. Whenever I have any questions, they are quick to lend a hand and offer support. The social life here is fantastic, and it’s a great opportunity to experience the true spirit of Podlasie. We’ve had amazing integrative trips, such as to Białowieża, and we’re soon going to Suprasl. I’ve also had the chance to explore traditional Podlaskie cuisine, which has been a delightful experience. I’m really looking forward to the rest of my time here!

title: Katarzyna (Kasia) Sidorczuk
text:
Biography
Hi! My name is Katarzyna Sidorczuk and I’m a bioinformatician interested in gut microbiome and use of machine learning for analysis of biological data.
During my PhD I worked with BioGenies and created multiple tools for prediction of peptide activity and protein localization. This led us to the work on negative data sampling for AMP prediction in which we showed that commonly used strategies introduce significance bias and leads to unreliable benchmarks.
Currently, I’m a postdoc in the Hildebrand group at the Quadram Institute, where I work with strain-resolved metagenomics. I’m interested in evolution of gut microbiota, how microbes are transferred between family members, and what are the factors that contribute to successful colonization and persistence.

title: About BioGenies
text:
What brings us together


01 / MOLECULES

How do proteins interact and assemble?
We investigate amyloid aggregation, its modulators and the interactions that shape protein behaviour, connecting sequence and structure with experiments.
Amyloids & aggregation · Phase separation



02 / DATA

How can we learn more from omics data?
We develop approaches to missing values and multiomics analysis, with an emphasis on comparing methods and making analyses reproducible.
Missing-value imputation · HDX-MS



03 / METHODS

How do we turn research into useful tools?
We combine curated biological knowledge, statistical modelling and machine learning in resources that other researchers can explore and reuse.
Software & databases · Antimicrobial peptides





PEOPLE MAKE THE SCIENCE

A shared curiosity, across institutions.
Our work grows through conversations, shared experiments and the different perspectives of our team, collaborators and guest researchers. Conferences and research exchanges help us build those connections; time together outside the lab matters too.

text: M-ERA.NET Call 2025 – Functional materials    Duration: 36 months · TRL 1 → 3    Coordinator: Medical University of Białystok, Poland

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Project overview
FIBREA tackles a central challenge in functional materials: how to design amyloid-based biomaterials rationally, rather than by trial and error.
We focus on curli-based functional amyloid materials (CFAMs), engineered variants of CsgA that:

self-assemble into fibrils with controllable morphology

remain compatible with bacterial secretion and intracellular inhibition

carry modular functional domains such as fluorophores or enzymes

The core idea is to learn a molecular grammar that links CFAM sequence features to fibril properties, co-assembly behavior, and production constraints.

Project at a glance

Acronym: FIBREA

Call: M-ERA.NET 2025 – functional materials

Duration: 36 months

TRL: 1 → 3

Main outputs:

Molecular grammar for CFAM design

Coarse-grained simulation framework (CALVADOS-based)

Optimized bacterial expression system

Fluorescent and catalytic CFAM prototypes

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Objectives

FIBREA builds a full design–build–test–learn loop for amyloid materials.


Develop a generalizable molecular grammar for stable CFAMs with tunable self-assembly.
Encode compatibility with:

curli secretion machinery (CsgEFG)
intracellular chaperones (CsgC, Spy)

Model CFAM assembly and inhibition using coarse-grained simulations (CALVADOS).
Optimize a bacterial expression system for high-yield CFAM production.
Demonstrate:

fluorescent CFAMs (GFP/YFP, including FRET-based co-assembly)
enzymatic CFAMs for multi-step catalytic cascades.

Advance the overall system from TRL 1 to TRL 3.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Concept and approach

FIBREA combines AI, physics-based simulations and wet-lab validation into a single workflow.


Molecular grammar (WP1)

Conditional denoising diffusion model trained on > 43 000 curli operons.

Encodes secretion compatibility, inhibition susceptibility, and fibrillization behavior.

Coarse-grained simulations (WP2)

CALVADOS used to simulate nucleation, growth, and polymorphism of CFAM fibrils.

Outputs structural descriptors (contact maps, stiffness, solvent exposure) feeding back into the grammar.

Expression and production (WP3)

Artificial gene design, codon optimization, fermentation strategy comparison, purification workflows.

Structural and biophysical validation (WP4)

ThT, Congo Red, Amytracker, CD, FTIR, TEM, AFM, cryo-EM.

In vitro testing of CsgC variants as inhibitors.

Functional CFAMs (WP5)

Fluorescent CFAMs for tracking and FRET analyses.

Dual-enzyme CFAMs as molecular assembly lines.


Only independently reproduced fibrillization results (Lithuanian labs) are used to refine the grammar, enforcing robustness.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Impact



 Scientific


Establishes design rules linking sequence → structure → function in amyloid materials.

Bridges machine learning, coarse-grained physics, and experiments.

Provides new insight into the curli system and CsgC-mediated inhibition.




 Economic


Lays the foundation for industrial CFAM applications: biosensing, catalysis, filtration, remediation.

Enables bio-based, programmable materials as alternatives to petroleum-derived polymers.




 Societal and environmental


Promotes biodegradable, low-toxicity materials from microbial systems.

Implements FAIR data, Open Science, and Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI).

Engages the public to show amyloids beyond their disease associations.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Consortium

FIBREA unites complementary expertise across bioinformatics, simulations, amyloid biology and synthetic biology.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Work packages

The work plan is organized into six interlinked WPs, forming a closed design–build–test–learn loop.




WP1


Design of the molecular grammar for CFAMs


Lead: PL · Type: research (TRL 1–2)


 AI and sequence design



Define biological constraints for secretion-competent constructs.


Learn CsgA variability and co-evolution with CsgC.


Develop conditional diffusion models for CFAM design.


Integrate feedback from simulations (WP2) and experiments (WP3–5).





WP2


Coarse-grained modeling of CFAMs


Lead: PL and ES · Type: research (TRL 1–2)


 CALVADOS



Set up CALVADOS simulations for CFAMs and inhibitors.


Screen engineered sequences in silico.


Extract structural descriptors for morphology and stability.


Calibrate against data from WP3 and WP4.





WP3


Optimization of the CFAM expression system


Lead: TR · Type: development (TRL 2–3)


 Bioprocess



Select host systems and design synthetic genes.


Optimize codon usage and expression constructs.


Compare batch vs continuous fermentation.


Improve purification and confirm functional integrity.





WP4


Assessment of uniform amyloid fibrillation


Lead: LT · Type: research (TRL 2–3)


 Structure



Biophysical assays (ThT, Congo Red, Amytracker, CD, FTIR).


TEM and AFM imaging of fibrils.


Cryo-EM structures of selected CFAM fibrils.


Inhibition studies with CsgC variants.





WP5


Harnessing material properties of CFAMs


Lead: ES · Type: development and demo (TRL 3)


 Function



Assess amyloid aggregation of functional CFAM fusions.


Validate GFP/YFP-based co-assembly and FRET.


Demonstrate dual-enzyme CFAM catalytic cascades.


Test inter-lab reproducibility of fibrillization and activity.





WP6


Consortium management and dissemination


Lead: PL


 Coordination



Scientific, administrative, and financial coordination.


Mattermost-based internal communication and data sharing.


Open Science, FAIR data, and RRI implementation.


Website, outreach, and training for early-career researchers.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Sustainability, RRI and data management

Sustainability:

Protein-based, biodegradable materials; microbial expression; potential for circular use.

Focus on low-energy, resource-efficient production strategies.

RRI and ethics:

Ethical review of experimental activities where required.

Biosecurity risk assessment aligned with EU and national regulations.

Public engagement on the constructive uses of amyloids.

Data and open science:

FAIR-compliant data, with deposition to public repositories (e.g. Zenodo, NCBI).

Code release (e.g. GitHub) under permissive licenses.

Documentation following the DOME recommendations for machine learning in life sciences.

title: Functional Interfaces and Biomolecular Rules for Engineered Amyloids
text:
Publications and outputs
A detailed list will be maintained as the project progresses. Planned outputs include:

Articles on:

CFAM molecular grammar and generative modeling

CALVADOS-based CFAM simulations

Structural and functional characterization of CFAMs

Conference presentations and workshops.
Open-source tools and curated datasets.

title: What happens when data go missing?
text: A missing measurement is a gap in our knowledge. Try filling a few gaps and see how the choice of method changes the answer.

title: What happens when data go missing?
text:
What does this tell us?
Here we know the original values because we deliberately hid them. That lets us measure the error. In a real experiment, the missing values are unknown, so the reason they are missing and the assumptions behind an algorithm matter.
This is a learning example with synthetic data and three simple methods. Its rankings describe this example and this hidden set. They are not the published imputomics benchmark or a recommendation for analysing a real dataset.

title: Big annoucement!
text:
Amyloids are proteins implicated in numerous serious diseases, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Creutzfeldt-Jakob’s disease, and type 2 diabetes. These proteins are known for their ability to self-aggregate into unique supramolecular fibrils, a process that plays a critical role in disease progression.
Our team has previously developed AmyloGraph, database of amyloid interactions, which you can explore here. In this new phase of our research, we aim to take AmyloGraph to the next level. We will design and implement machine learning-based tools to analyze the data more effectively and revamp the user interface to make it easier for researchers to access the latest information.
But that’s not all. The data collected during this project will be used to train predictive models, with the ultimate goal of designing new chemical compounds that can inhibit amyloid self-aggregation. These compounds hold great promise for the treatment of various amyloid-related diseases.

title: PTBI 2024 Conference wrap-up
text:
And that’s a wrap for the PTBI 2024 conference! It was filled with insightful talks 🎤, a vibrant poster session 📊, and, of course, great company 🤝. From exciting discussions to memorable reunions, here’s are some of the highlights!


Kasia and Michał kicked off the event with their early arrivals. 
Jarek, Krysia and Weronika joined shortly after, ready for action and collaboration. 
Meanwhile, Valen had the special opportunity to meet with the Undersecretary of State in the Ministry of Science in the evening, making it a memorable encounter! 



We attended a series of fascinating presentations throughout the event. But the standout? Kasia’s talk on Strain-resolved metagenomics in analysis of gut microbiota dynamics within families stole the show, at least for us! 
Of course, we also couldn’t miss Weronika’s impressive poster presentation! 



After a packed first day, we set out to grab some ice cream to unwind, but, to our surprise, every shop was closed! During the adventure of hunting for an open place, we even temporarily “lost” Jarek and Krysia for a bit! 😅




And finally, the ultimate highlight—our fun-filled BioGenies reunion! Catching up with old friends and creating new memories was the perfect end to an incredible conference.




Our next big adventure? The HUPO 2024 conference in Dresden! You’ll find Michał, Jarek, Krysia, Weronika, and Oriol representing us there. We can’t wait to see you there!

But that’s not all. The data collected during this project will be used to train predictive models, with the ultimate goal of designing new chemical compounds that can inhibit amyloid self-aggregation. These compounds hold great promise for the treatment of various amyloid-related diseases.

title: HUPO 2024 Conference Wrap-Up
text:
Our BioGenies team: Michał, Jarek, Krysia, Weronika and Oriol, had an unforgettable week at HUPO 2024 in Dresden! Here’s the highlight reel:


We started the week with a stroll to explore the conference site and snapped a photo of the iconic Yenidze, a former cigarette factory with a unique design 🕌.

That evening, we picked up Oriol from the airport ✈️ and headed to Sophienkeller to dive into local Dresden delicacies 🥨🍖.




Sunday night kicked off with the opening ceremony and welcome reception 🍾, followed by an Early Career Researchers Networking Night. Despite the darkness on our boat tour 🌌, we made the most of it by networking with fellow researchers. The highlight? Watching as they joined two boats together – an unexpected twist to the night! 🚢




Monday saw some friendly rivalry when Jarek and Krysia discovered an air hockey table! After an intense game, it ended in a tie 🤝.

Later, Krysia reunited with our colleague Dominik in the plenary hall,

and Jarek, Weronika, and Oriol snapped some fun group photos 📸.




Each of us had poster sessions on different days, and it was exciting to see such strong interest in our research 🧬📈. The steady traffic at our posters highlighted the growing excitement around our work!




Between sessions, we sampled even more homemade Dresden dishes – fueling our research discussions and conference exploration 🥘💪.




We carved out some time to visit the famous Bastei Bridge. Though the heavy fog limited the view 🌫️, it added a mystique that made for an unforgettable (and chilly) adventure! 🏞️
 



Oriol’s return flight was suddenly canceled due to an airport strike 😱. But no worries – Michał, Jarek, and Weronika swooped in 🚗, picking him up from his hotel to drive him back to the airport.



After the conference wrapped up, Weronika and Jarek spent Friday exploring the beautiful Dresdner Zwinger – a perfect way to close out a memorable week of science and sightseeing 🏛️✨.

Thanks, HUPO 2024, for the inspiring talks, new connections, and unforgettable memories! Until next time, Dresden! 🇩🇪💫

title: Welcome Eva Arribas to the Lab!
text:
We’re excited to welcome Eva to our lab! Eva joins us from the Institut de Biotecnologia i de Biomedicina at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, where she completed her master’s research in Salvador Ventura’s lab 🎓🔬. She’s here as part of her Erasmus traineeship, diving into the fascinating world of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)!


Eva arrived on 1st November, a big holiday in Poland 🇵🇱, which made it an especially busy day for travel. With everything bustling and crowded, even trains to Białystok were packed! 🚆 So, we took a trip to the airport to greet her and ensure she had a smooth arrival – and to give her a warm BioGenies welcome 🌟.




During her traineeship, Eva will be working on LLPS, a critical phenomenon in biomolecular condensates that has big implications for understanding cell organization and disease processes. We’re looking forward to the fresh insights and new ideas she’ll bring to our LLPS projects!
Eva, we’re thrilled to have you with us – welcome to the team! 🎉

title: Farewell to Eva, our first departing Erasmus+ student! 🎓💙
text:
This past week was bittersweet as we said goodbye to Eva, our second Erasmus student but the first to leave. Her time with us was filled with science, fun, and unforgettable moments, and we made sure to give her a proper BioGenies send-off! 🚀


🟢 Thursday – Pierogi, kartacze and potato grandma 🤭 feast! 🥟 A classic Polish experience for a proper farewell.


🟢 Friday – Sushi lunch 🍣 followed by the 4th International Karaoke Night at UMB! 🎤🌍


🟢 Sunday – An adventure in Białowieża, walking the route to Jagiełło oak, followed by a delicious meal at Fanaberia restaurant 🍽️.



🟢 Tuesday – Our last pancake night 🥞 with Jarek, Ronja, Eva, and Maria.
 Eva ordered sweet pancakes and managed to eat half, which we count as a victory! 🎉


🟢 Final goodbye – On Wednesday, we went together to the train station to say our last goodbye in Białystok. 💔🚆




Eva didn’t leave BioGenies empty-handed — she left us some nice gifts! 🎁 We’re grateful for everything she brought to our lab and will truly miss her.




It is always sad to see another great researcher leaving academia. Eva has an incredible mind, and the academic world is losing a talented scientist. But wherever she goes next, we know she will make a difference and continue to excel! 💙
Eva, we wish you all the best in your future adventures! 🚀💙

title: 🎉 OneTick project awarded MSCA Staff Exchanges grant!
text:
Just a few days after celebrating Jarek’s ERA Fellowship, we received another incredible notification from the European Commission.



Not only is this our first project of this kind, we’re the only project coordinated from Poland among a total 19 proposals submitted by Polish-led consortia! 😲
👏 Huge congratulations to Michał, who led the application and tirelessly coordinated with all the partners. Jarek and Valen were deeply involved in writing and structuring the proposal, but the heavy lifting, all those calls and negotiations, was on Michał’s shoulders. And he nailed it 💪



OneTick investigates tick-borne diseases using a One Health approach, linking human, animal, and environmental health.



Impact of climate change on tick behavior and presence in urban and peri-urban areas (parks, gardens, playgrounds)
Use of AI-based modeling, epidemiology and field ecology to:

Improve risk assessment
Understand tick distribution
Inform control strategies






The project brings together 13 partners from 10 countries, including:

🧭 Medical University of Białystok 🇵🇱
🧪 Tick-radar GmbH 🇩🇪

🧬 FUNDACION RIOJA SALUD 🇪🇸

🎓 Södertörn University 🇸🇪

🏥 Rigshospitalet 🇩🇰

💊 Pfizer 🇦🇹

🧠 Freie Universität Berlin 🇩🇪

🐾 University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca 🇷🇴

🏥 Region Jönköpings län 🇸🇪

🏥 Sørlandet sykehus HF 🇳🇴

🧫 RIVM National Institute for Public Health and the Environment 🇳🇱

🔬 Biologické centrum AV ČR, v.v.i. 🇨🇿



We’re beyond excited to kick off this cross-disciplinary, cross-sector collaboration to tackle a growing public health challenge! 💚
Stay tuned for updates, ticks don’t rest, and neither do we 🕷️🌍

We made new connections with fellow researchers and, importantly, stayed cool in the AC!

title: Michał talks reproducibility at Bioinformatics Community Meetup #5 💻🧬 🇵🇱
text:
Michał represented BioGenies at Bioinformatics Community Meetup #5 in Kraków 🇵🇱, joining the expert panel:
The discussion focused on a topic very close to our everyday work: how to make bioinformatics research actually reproducible. That means not only producing nice figures and significant p-values, but also sharing code and data properly, avoiding statistical and logical pitfalls, and making sure others can really build on the results 🧬📊✅.
Michał joined panelists from academia and industry, bringing his perspective from Medical University of Białystok and Vilnius University. The panel also looked at what happens when unreliable research leaves academia and becomes the foundation for real products or analyses, where bad reproducibility can become a much more expensive problem 💸😅.
For BioGenies, this is a particularly relevant topic: with so much of our work involving machine learning, benchmarking, data analysis and software development, reproducibility is not an optional extra. It is part of doing the science properly.
Huge thanks to the Bioinformatics Community PL team for inviting Michał to the discussion! 🤝🚀

Used for direct visualization of aggregates and fibrils.

title: Can ML predictors detect mislabeled amyloids? 🧠🧬
text:
⚠️ Massive misannotation discovered
Among 24 experimentally tested “outlier” peptides:

17 were actually misannotated in databases

That means:
👉 the ML model was often RIGHT
👉 the database labels were WRONG 😅

title: Can ML predictors detect mislabeled amyloids? 🧠🧬
text:
🤖 AmyloGram resisted overfitting
Even though those mislabeled peptides were:
👉 already present in the training set,
AmyloGram still identified many as suspicious.
This is a huge result.
It suggests:
🧠 ML models can sometimes act as quality-control filters for biological databases.

title: Can ML predictors detect mislabeled amyloids? 🧠🧬
text:
🧪 IR microscopy outperformed ATR-FTIR
The authors conclude that:
👉 IR microscopy was generally more reliable
because ATR-FTIR could be influenced by:

water interactions
sample thickness
surface effects

title: Can ML predictors detect mislabeled amyloids? 🧠🧬
text:
🧬 Oligomers complicate annotations
Some sequences behaved differently depending on the method used.
Example:

SFLIFL formed oligomers but not mature fibrils

This explains why database labels may become inconsistent.

title: Can ML predictors detect mislabeled amyloids? 🧠🧬
text:

This paper is a great example of:
👉 weak supervision in biology.
The training labels are not absolute truth.

computational tools can help detect inconsistencies

The research question
AmyloGraph began as a resource for amyloid–amyloid interactions. This project extends its scope to a wider range of self-assembly modulators and the experimental context in which they act. The resulting curated evidence supports models that go beyond predicting whether a protein aggregates, towards understanding how its aggregation can be changed.

02 / RESEARCH AIM

Predict modulation
Train machine learning models to predict how a modulator affects amyloid aggregation.



03 / RESEARCH AIM

Explore new modulators
Develop generative models and assess proposed modulators computationally and experimentally.

text:
The research question
Missing values can change the conclusions drawn from omics experiments, yet the best imputation method depends on the dataset and the analytical question. Building on the imputomics web server and R package, this project broadens the framework from metabolomics to multiomics and makes methods easier to compare through common interfaces and curated benchmarks.

section: What the project sets out to do

What the project sets out to do


01 / RESEARCH AIM

Curate methods and datasets
Review imputation algorithms and annotate their assumptions, applications and omics-specific characteristics.



02 / RESEARCH AIM

Build a common interface
Develop a standardised wrapper for methods across genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics.



03 / RESEARCH AIM

Compare what matters
Benchmark methods using error, correlation, interpretability and downstream tasks, and share an open repository of algorithms and datasets.

title: The science, in plain language
text: What was the problem? What did we build? What did we learn? Meet the questions behind three of our research tools.

title: The science, in plain language
section: What should fill a gap in your data?
text:
What should fill a gap in your data?

IMPUTOMICS / METABOLOMICS


A blank measurement is a question, not a number.


What was the problem?
Metabolomics experiments measure small molecules in biological samples, but some measurements are missing. Researchers can estimate the gaps using many different algorithms, spread across packages that can be difficult to install, compare and run consistently.


What did we build?
imputomics brings multiple imputation methods into one R package and web application, with a common interface and a benchmarking workflow.


What did we learn?
The published benchmark found differences in accuracy, speed and reliability across methods and missing-data scenarios. Choosing a method means considering the dataset and why values are missing. The paper provides evidence to guide that choice.


Who can use it?
Researchers working with incomplete metabolomics data, including those who prefer a web interface to writing R code.
Try a demo Open imputomics ↗
Read the original paper, Bioinformatics (2024) · Full group story · Missing-data research

title: The science, in plain language
section: What happens when amyloid proteins meet?
text:
What happens when amyloid proteins meet?

AMYLOGRAPH / PROTEIN AGGREGATION


Connecting experiments that used to live in separate papers.


What was the problem?
Amyloid-forming proteins can affect one another’s aggregation. Evidence for these interactions was scattered across experimental papers, using different terms and descriptions.


What did we build?
AmyloGraph collects experimentally studied interactions in a searchable database, with a shared vocabulary and links back to the evidence. The published release brought together 883 interactions between 46 proteins or peptides.


What did we learn?
The literature describes different kinds of effects, including faster or slower fibril formation and interactions involving physical binding. Recording these details separately helps researchers compare what experiments actually report.


Who can use it?
Researchers exploring amyloid interactions, looking for previous experiments or assembling evidence for new questions.
Explore AmyloGraph ↗
Read the original paper, Nucleic Acids Research (2023 issue) · Full group story · Amyloid research

title: The science, in plain language
section: How can we follow a protein’s changing behaviour?
text:
How can we follow a protein’s changing behaviour?

HADEX2 / STRUCTURAL PROTEOMICS


Making a complex experiment easier to analyse together.


What was the problem?
Proteins move and change. Hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS, helps investigate that behaviour by measuring deuterium uptake over time. Its results span protein regions, time points, biological conditions, charge states and repeated measurements.


What did we build?
HaDeX2 brings statistical analysis and visualisation across those five dimensions into an R package and web application.


What did we learn?
Considering these dimensions together helps researchers compare uptake patterns and biological conditions while accounting for experimental variability. HaDeX2 provides a common analysis framework for examining those comparisons.


Who can use it?
Experimental and computational researchers analysing HDX-MS experiments and investigating protein structure, dynamics and interactions.
Open HaDeX2 ↗

title: Amyloids & protein aggregation
text: How do proteins assemble into amyloid structures, and what happens when different amyloids meet?

title: Amyloids & protein aggregation
text:
Why amyloids matter
Amyloids are ordered protein assemblies with a characteristic cross-β structure. They are studied in the context of protein misfolding and disease, but they also have biological functions: bacterial curli, for example, contribute to the extracellular matrix of biofilms. Understanding amyloids means looking at both their molecular structure and the biological setting in which they form.
Aggregation is also an interaction problem. One protein can alter the aggregation of another, and the outcome depends on the proteins, experimental conditions and the measurements used. Bringing those observations together makes it easier to compare findings that would otherwise remain scattered across the literature.

title: Amyloids & protein aggregation
text:
Questions we explore

How can we organise evidence about interactions between different amyloid-forming proteins?
What makes an amyloid dataset useful for prediction and comparison?
How can computational predictions and experimental measurements inform each other?

title: Amyloids & protein aggregation
text:
Our approach
We connect literature curation, databases, computational analysis and experimental evidence. AmyloGraph organises reports of amyloid–amyloid interactions, while our work on prediction and annotation examines how reliably sequence-based models describe amyloid behaviour.
We also study the resources and experimental methods used across the field. Clear annotations and complementary measurements help distinguish an observed interaction from a proposed mechanism. Our publication stories below explain the questions, methods and limitations behind these projects.

title: Liquid–liquid phase separation
text: Making sense of biomolecular condensates through carefully curated data and more informative benchmarks.

title: Liquid–liquid phase separation
text:
Organisation without a membrane
Cells can concentrate proteins and nucleic acids into assemblies known as biomolecular condensates. Liquid–liquid phase separation is one mechanism that can produce such compartments: interactions among molecules favour a concentrated phase alongside a more dilute one. The behaviour depends on molecular composition and experimental conditions.
For computational studies, the challenge is not simply to decide whether a protein has ever appeared in a condensate. A protein that helps drive phase separation may play a different role from one recruited into an existing assembly. Useful datasets need to preserve those distinctions and the evidence behind them.

title: Liquid–liquid phase separation
text:
Questions we explore

How should we distinguish proteins that drive phase separation from proteins recruited into condensates?
Which negative examples make a benchmark informative?
How well do prediction methods generalise across different datasets?

title: Liquid–liquid phase separation
text:
Our approach
Our work focuses on the data used to study and predict phase separation. We bring together curated protein datasets and examine how the choice of positive and negative examples changes the evaluation of prediction tools.
The aim is to make comparisons easier to interpret and reproduce. Distinguishing drivers, clients and negative examples helps researchers ask more precise questions about what a model has learned, rather than treating every condensate-associated protein as the same kind of example.
